g.text: Stacks & Queues — plates you pile, lines you join
Two of the simplest structures, and two everyday pictures. A stack is a pile of plates — you
add and take only from the top. A queue is a line at the coffee shop — you join the back and
the front is served first. Push, pop, enqueue and dequeue — one animated move at a time.
Push, pop, peek — last in, first out
A stack of plates: you add and remove from the top only. The last plate on is the first one off. That is the
same stack Python used for the call stack in recursion — now you are holding it directly.
Enqueue, dequeue — first in, first out
A line at the coffee shop: you join at the back and the person at the front is served first. No
cutting in — everyone waits their turn. First in line, first served.
Built from a list — and the one trap to avoid
A stack is just a Python list — add and remove at the end, both O(1). A queue looks the same, but removing from the front of a list is slow.
Stack on a list — end operations
You already use these every day
Every edit pushed on a stack; Ctrl-Z pops the last one.
Each page you visit is pushed; Back pops to the previous.
The plates you watched pile up were literally a stack.
Push each opener, pop on its closer — editors check code this way.
Documents print in the order you sent them — first in, first out.
Servers line up jobs and handle them fairly, in arrival order.
Exploring level by level uses a queue — coming up next.
"Your call is held in a queue" — the same idea, out loud.
Looking back: the call stack you met in recursion is exactly this stack — nesting dolls pile up the same way plates do.
Looking forward: exploring a tree or graph wide (BFS) uses a queue; going deep (DFS) uses a stack.
